title: Jansenius with Scotus: the necessity in such acts is concomitant, not antecedent
source_text: XXXI. Etenim quae tum reperitur in voluntate necessitas, ut verbis Scoti mentem suam exprimit, non est praevia ad voluntatem, ut voluntas intelligatur cadere sub necessitate, tanquam impellente in actum, & figente in actum, quoniam si sic esset, voluntas ageretur & non ageret, nec staret in tali actu libertas. Sed est necessitas concomitans, ita quod ipsa intelligatur cadere sub voluntate, sic quod voluntas, propter firmitatem libertatis suae, sibi ipsi necessitatem imponit in eliciendo actum, & in perseverando, sive figendo, se in actum. De Grat. Chr. Salvat. lib. 6. cap. 37.
pass_a_gloss: For the necessity which is then found in the will, as he expresses his mind in the words of Scotus, is not prior to the will, so that the will is understood to fall under necessity, as impelling into the act, and fixing in the act, since if it were so, the will would be acted on and would not act, nor would liberty stand in such an act. But it is a concomitant necessity, so that it is understood to fall under the will, so that the will, because of the firmness of its liberty, imposes necessity on itself in eliciting the act, and in persevering, or fixing, itself in the act. On the Grace of Christ the Saviour book 6. chap. 37.
pass_b_english: The necessity then present in the will, as he puts it in Scotus's words, 'does not come before the will, so that the will would be understood to fall under a necessity that drives it into the act and fixes it there. If that were so, the will would be acted upon and would not act, and freedom could not remain in such an act.

'It is a concomitant necessity, understood to fall under the will. The will, through the firmness of its freedom, lays necessity on itself in bringing forth its act and in persevering in it, that is, in fixing itself on the act.' (On the Grace of Christ the Saviour, book 6, chapter 37.)

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.
